title: SDK acceptance gateways & telemetry contracts for multi-language clients
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Background:
Many enterprise customers request language bindings and client libraries with consistent auth and streaming ergonomics. During onboarding we see recurring integration friction: mismatched telemetry formats, unclear session-resume handshake semantics, and inconsistent error codes across language clients. These cause delayed proof-of-concepts, increased support cycles, and occasional data-plane flips when customers attempt to plug third-party SDKs into Dedicated/Private deployments.

Problem statement:
We lack a lightweight, testable mechanism to validate that a client library (or customer-owned adapter) meets Redwood's runtime expectations before customers commit to Dedicated or Private installs. Without this, we accept brittle integrations and rely on ad-hoc engineering fixes.

Goals:
- Define a minimal "acceptance gateway" spec that client libraries can run against to verify auth flows, streaming checkpoints, backpressure behavior, and telemetry contract compliance.
- Create a reference test harness and a set of small, language-agnostic canonical scenarios (connect, refresh token, stream interrupt/reconnect, KV cache hinting) for customer SDKs.
- Reduce enterprise onboarding time by 30% for client-led integrations and cut triage back-and-forth on auth/streaming issues by 50%.
- Provide clear error categories and recommended remediation steps for common failures.

Non-goals:
- Full replacement of SDKs or language-specific API ergonomics (we still expect SDKs to provide idiomatic surface areas).
- Implementing all telemetry backfills for historical customers — focus on forward-compatible contracts.

Proposed approach:
1) Acceptance gateway spec: document a small HTTP/gRPC shim that validates a client adapter against: token exchange flows (bearer, mTLS, delegated), streaming frame semantics (resume tokens, partial frames, truncation), and telemetry envelope format (minimum fields: client_id, sdk_version, sequence_id, event_type). Failure modes should map to a short taxonomy (auth_failure, handshake_mismatch, backpressure_violation, telemetry_mismatch).
2) Reference harness: produce a lightweight CLI tool (go/rust/python) that runs canonical scenarios against the shim and produces a human-friendly report and machine-readable artifact (signed attestation blob) for sales/solutions to accept.
3) Language adapters: produce minimal examples for Node, Python, Java showing how to integrate with the shim and how to produce compliant telemetry. These are example code only; adoption by official SDK maintainers is separate work.
4) Integrate into onboarding flow: sales/solutions run the harness as an early gate. For Dedicated/Private installs, require an attestation blob in the onboarding checklist or mark as "engineering-assisted" if failing.

Acceptance criteria:
- Public spec doc published in Confluence: /confluence/Redwood/SDK-Acceptance-Gateway (draft).
- CLI harness v0.1 released in github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-acceptance, passing smoke tests in CI.
- Three language examples (node, python, java) demonstrating the four canonical scenarios.
- Onboarding playbook updated and tested with 2 recent enterprise pilots.

Metrics to track:
- Time from first SDK ask to Verified Attestation (target: reduce by 30%).
- Number of enterprise onboarding handoffs flagged as "engineering-assisted" before vs after feature (target: reduce by 50%).
- Failure taxonomy distribution (auth vs streaming vs telemetry) to prioritize SDK product improvements.

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Customers will view the attestation as extra friction. Mitigation: keep scenarios small and runnable locally; provide partner-run options.
- Risk: Multiple language variants cause spec drift. Mitigation: keep telemetry contract minimal and use CI tests to enforce.
